name: Gum massage / Stillman technique

lead: The Stillman technique is a toothbrushing method built around gentle action at the gumline, sometimes described as gum massage. People use it hoping for healthier-looking, less inflamed gums that frame the smile.

Proponents say stimulating the gums improves circulation and plaque removal where the teeth meet the gum. The sources reviewed do not include trials of the method; Wikipedia notes that dental technique advice has been inconsistent and that lay people clean at most about 40% of tooth margins at the gumline.

paras: Users angle the brush at the gumline and work with light pressure as part of normal daily brushing, or add gentle fingertip or brush massage along the gums. It is folded into the usual morning and evening routine alongside flossing.

General dental guidance cautions against pressing hard on teeth and gums, which can irritate the tissue. Anyone with bleeding, swollen or receding gums is generally advised to have a dentist assess them.

chain: Better plaque control and circulation claimed
angle.text: Gentle gumline brushing or massage is discussed online as a way to improve plaque control and circulation, so gums look healthier around the teeth. Trials of the Stillman method were not found in the sources reviewed.

lead: The Stillman technique is a toothbrushing method named for a dental researcher, associated with gentle gum stimulation or massage alongside cleaning at the gumline. Gum massage is discussed in online circles as a way to improve gum health.

The pages consulted for this article do not describe the Stillman method or gum massage, so evidence is limited here. Wikipedia notes that technique advice from dental associations, companies and textbooks has been inconsistent, and that lay people clean at most about 40% of tooth margins at the gumline.[1]

paras: General guidance reported includes avoiding hard pressure and horizontal scrubbing at the necks of teeth.[1] Harder brushes remove plaque more efficiently but stress teeth and gums more; a 2011 study rated a medium-to-soft brush used longer as the best compromise.[1]
